provenance.other: “a division among” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, John 7:43 and John 9:16, and both are the same formula about the same crowd — 'there was a division among the people because of him', 'there was a division among them'. John 10:19 reads 'a division therefore again among the Jews' and so falls outside the string. Mosiah 19:2's 'there began to be a division among the remainder of the people' has John 7:43's noun, preposition and object.
provenance.significance: John's divisions are always caused by a person and always split a crowd into those who accept him and those who do not; the Book of Mormon's is caused by the same thing one chapter later, since the 'lesser part' at 19:3 is the faction that has heard Abinadi and Alma. Taking the phrase from John rather than from the KJV's political vocabulary makes the coup at Mosiah 19 a religious schism with an army attached, which is what the narrative in fact reports.

19:2.note: 'The forces of the king were small, having been reduced, and there began to be a division among the remainder of the people.' A four-word run whose only KJV homes are two verses of the same Johannine formula. Catalogued at moderate confidence because 'division among the people' is unremarkable English; what raises it is that the KJV reserves the phrase for exactly this situation, a population split by a preacher, and that is the situation Mosiah 18 has just produced.
19:2.text: So there was a division among the people because of him.

provenance.other: “breathing out threatenings” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 9:1, and the noun itself is nearly as rare: 'threatenings' occurs in exactly two, Acts 4:29 and Acts 9:1. The 1830 first edition spells it 'threatnings', which is the KJV's own contracted orthography surviving in the running text and lost in later editions.
provenance.significance: Acts 9:1's phrase belongs to Saul of Tarsus on the road to Damascus — the persecutor a verse away from becoming the apostle. Mosiah 17:2 has already put Acts 7:58's young man at Abinadi's execution, and this catalogue reads Alma as standing in that position; two chapters later the book takes the next stage of the same man's story and gives it to the party that will overthrow king Noah. Whether the writer meant the two borrowings to be read together, the effect is that the Book of Mormon narrates its own reformation in the vocabulary of Saul's — first the young man at the stoning, then the breathing out of threatenings — and reverses the polarity, since here the threatenings are directed at the persecuting king rather than at the church.

19:3.note: 'And the lesser part began to breathe out threatnings against the king, and there began to be a great contention among them.' A three-word KJV singleton in its exact grammatical form, and the 1830 spelling preserves the KJV's contraction. Note the transposition: in Acts the participle describes a man moving against the disciples, in Mosiah it describes the faction that has just been made disciples moving against the state.
19:3.text: And Saul, yet breathing out threatenings and slaughter against the disciples of the Lord, went unto the high priest,

provenance.other: “drew his sword” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 26:51 — the disciple in Gethsemane who strikes the high priest's servant, and whom Jesus rebukes two verses later. The Book of Mormon's own Gideon is named for the judge of Judges 6–8, whose one sword-drawing scene is a negative: Judges 8:20's 'the youth drew not his sword: for he feared'.
provenance.alternative: 'Drew his sword' is ordinary narrative English and its absence elsewhere in the KJV may be accidental — the KJV usually writes 'drew a sword' or 'drew out his sword'.
provenance.significance: The two candidate backgrounds pull opposite ways and that is what makes the verse worth an entry. The KJV's only man who draws his sword does so in defence of a condemned prophet, against the servants of a high priest, and is told to put it up; the KJV's Gideon presides over a son who will not draw his. Mosiah's Gideon draws his against a king who has burned a prophet, and the narrative neither rebukes him nor lets him finish — 19:6 stops the blow with a Lamanite army. The Book of Mormon has taken the sword-drawing of the passion, which is forbidden, and suspended the question rather than answering it.

19:4.note: 'He drew his sword and swore in his wrath, that he would slay the king.' A KJV singleton, but a short one, and the sense is not transferred whole — this is why the row is an echo rather than an allusion. Recorded chiefly because Gideon's name makes the Judges background unavoidable and the Judges background says the opposite.
19:4.whyNot: Three ordinary words. The KJV's failure to use them elsewhere is a fact about its idiom rather than a mark of distinctiveness, and nothing else in Mosiah 19:4 touches Gethsemane.
19:4.text: And, behold, one of them which were with Jesus stretched out his hand, and drew his sword, and struck a servant of the high priest’s, and smote off his ear.

provenance.route: Psalm 95:11 or Hebrews 3:11 → KJV → Book of Mormon; the verse cannot decide between them
provenance.other: “sware in my wrath” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Psalm 95:11 and Hebrews 3:11, which are the psalm and the epistle's quotation of it, and they are verbally identical at the phrase; “sworn in my wrath” occurs in exactly one, Hebrews 4:3. Swearing in wrath is otherwise God's act alone in the KJV. tools/mediation-check.py, run on Psalm 95:11 against Hebrews 3:11, finds no decisive divergence, and the reason is that the two agree at every word the Book of Mormon reproduces; the Book of Mormon's own preterite is 'swore', which is neither text's 'sware' nor Hebrews 4:3's 'sworn', so the form cannot be traced. `mediation` is recorded as uncertain on that basis rather than defaulted.
provenance.significance: Every KJV oath sworn in wrath is God's, and its content is always exclusion from rest — 'they shall not enter into my rest'. Gideon's oath is a man's, and its content is regicide. Read against the psalm the sentence is blasphemous by construction: a private citizen assumes the one formula the King James Bible reserves for divine judicial anger. Read against Hebrews 3–4, whose argument is that the wilderness generation lost its rest by rebellion, it is worse, because Gideon's people are a wilderness generation in rebellion against their king.

19:4.note: 'And he drew his sword and swore in his wrath, that he would slay the king.' Offered under CONVENTIONS §0a: the phrase is short and the transfer from God to a man is so complete that no reader would notice it, which is an argument against the borrowing and also the reason it is interesting if it is one. The mediation result is negative and is recorded as such.
19:4.whyNot: Four common words, and 'swore in his wrath' is idiomatic English independent of the KJV. Nothing else in the verse points at Psalm 95 or Hebrews.
19:4.text: Unto whom I sware in my wrath that they should not enter into my rest.

provenance.other: “top of the tower” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Judges 9:51, which is the tower of Thebez, the last of the three towers in the Abimelech narrative. Mosiah 19:5's king 'fled and ran and got upon the tower, which was near the temple' — Judges 9:46 has the men of Shechem entering 'an hold of the house of the god Berith', a tower attached to a temple, which is the only tower in the KJV so described.
provenance.significance: This is the chapter's controlling source and the name gives it away. Judges 9 is the story of Gideon's son Abimelech, who makes himself king over Israel by murder, is cursed by Jotham with fire ('let fire come out from Abimelech, and devour the men of Shechem ... and devour Abimelech'), burns a thousand people in a tower by a temple, and dies at a second tower when he is struck from above and, unable to face the shame of it, begs to be killed. Mosiah 19 redistributes every element and inverts the genealogy: the pursuer is called Gideon, the king who flees to the tower is the Abimelech, and the fire of Jotham's curse arrives at 19:20 on the king rather than from him. Reading the two together answers a question the Book of Mormon never asks aloud — why a man called Gideon should be the one to hunt a king up a tower. In Judges the tower-burner is Gideon's son; here Gideon is the one at the foot of the ladder.

19:5.note: 'He fled and ran and got upon the tower, which was near the temple. And Gideon pursued after him and was about to get upon the tower to slay the king.' The KJV has one 'top of the tower', one tower joined to a temple, and one narrative in which a usurping king, a man named Gideon and a death by fire all belong together — Judges 9. The Book of Mormon's version is that narrative with the roles reassigned, and the reassignment is legible only because the name has been kept.
19:5.text: But there was a strong tower within the city, and thither fled all the men and women, and all they of the city, and shut it to them, and gat them up to the top of the tower.

provenance.other: “the anguish of his soul” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 42:21, and the shorter “the anguish of” occurs in exactly two. Genesis 42:21 is Joseph's brothers in Egypt, twenty years on: 'We are verily guilty concerning our brother, in that we saw the anguish of his soul, when he besought us, and we would not hear.'
provenance.significance: The KJV's one anguish of the soul belongs to a man pleading for his life with his own kin, who hear him and refuse — and the verse is not the pleading itself but the memory of it, spoken by the men who refused, at the moment they realise they are being punished for it. Mosiah 19:7 gives that phrase to king Noah begging Gideon, and Gideon does what Joseph's brothers did not: he hears, and spares him. What follows is the point. The mercy is not the end of the story; 19:20 has Noah burned by his own people, and 19:24 has them return 'rejoicing'. The Book of Mormon has borrowed the vocabulary of a guilt that took twenty years to arrive and attached it to a reprieve that lasts thirteen verses, and it lets the reader supply the comparison. Note also 19:8's editorial line, 'the king was not so much concerned about his people, as he was about his own life' — which is exactly the accusation Genesis 42:21 has the brothers level at themselves.

19:7.note: 'And now the king cried out in the anguish of his soul, saying, Gideon, spare me, for the Lamanites are upon us, and they will destroy them; yea, they will destroy my people.' Five words from the KJV's only occurrence of the phrase, and the 1830 reading makes the sentence worse than the modern text does: 'they will destroy them' at the first clause, corrected to 'us' in 1920, has Noah beginning the plea by speaking of his people in the third person and only afterwards claiming them. The first edition's pronoun is the evidence for 19:8's verdict on him.
19:7.text: And they said one to another, We are verily guilty concerning our brother, in that we saw the anguish of his soul, when he besought us, and we would not hear; therefore is this distress come upon us.

provenance.other: “if I perish I perish” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Esther 4:16, the Bible's classic formula for choosing to share the fate of a threatened people rather than escape it. 'Perish with' is commoner — six verses — and the Book of Mormon's phrasing, 'had rather stay and perish with them', is its own.
provenance.significance: Esther's sentence is spoken by someone who could have survived by keeping quiet, and Ruth 1:17's 'where thou diest, will I die' by someone who could have gone home. Mosiah 19:12 divides a whole population by that choice in a single verse — 'there were many that would not leave them, but had rather stay and perish with them. And the rest left their wives and their children and fled' — and 19:19 shows the fugitives adopting it afterwards, swearing to return and 'also perish with them'. The chapter is testing every character against Esther's formula, and the men who fail it at 19:12 are the same men who at 19:20 burn the king who told them to run.

19:12.note: Recorded as an echo, not an allusion: no string is shared. What is shared is the KJV's one articulated form of the choice, and the Book of Mormon puts that choice at the exact hinge of its narrative, since the women who stay are the ones whose beauty saves the people at 19:14 and the men who run are the ones who kill the king at 19:20.
19:12.whyNot: A resemblance of situation with no verbal contact whatever. Solidarity with the doomed is a human commonplace and needs no source; the entry exists because Esther 4:16 is the KJV's only formulation of it and the chapter turns on the choice twice.
19:12.text: Go, gather together all the Jews that are present in Shushan, and fast ye for me, and neither eat nor drink three days, night or day: I also and my maidens will fast likewise; and so will I go in unto the king, which is not according to the law: and if I perish, I perish.

provenance.other: No phrase is shared. The KJV's own marker for the type-scene is “fair to look upon”, which occurs in exactly two verses, Genesis 24:16 and Genesis 26:7, the second of them Isaac's version of this same episode; Genesis 12:11 has 'a fair woman to look upon'. Mosiah 19:14 has 'they were charmed with the beauty of their women', which is not KJV diction at all.
provenance.significance: The patriarchal wife-sister scene has a fixed shape: a man enters a stronger people's territory, fears he will be killed, and survives because of his wife's beauty — 'they will kill me, but they will save thee alive ... that it may be well with me for thy sake; and my soul shall live because of thee'. Mosiah 19:11-15 runs the shape at national scale and moves the shame. Abraham arranges the deception himself and profits by it; Noah's men are ordered to abandon their wives outright, and it is the women who, unprompted, 'stand forth and plead' and save the people who stayed. The Genesis scene's discreditable bargain — a man's life bought with a woman's beauty — is exactly what happens here, and the Book of Mormon assigns the discredit to the men who fled rather than to the arrangement.

19:13.note: A figural link with no wording behind it, offered under CONVENTIONS §0a and marked kjvSpecific 'no' accordingly. It is included because the type-scene is one of the most recognisable in the Pentateuch, because Mosiah 19:11-15 reproduces its logic step for step, and because the chapter's judgment on the episode is only legible against it.
19:13.whyNot: Nothing verbal at all; and the Lamanites sparing captive women for their beauty needs no literary source, being a commonplace of war narrative. A reader who declines this row loses nothing from the chapter's other links.
19:13.text: Say, I pray thee, thou art my sister: that it may be well with me for thy sake; and my soul shall live because of thee.

provenance.other: “being a just man” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 1:19; the bare 'a just man' stands in eight. Matthew 1:19 is the only place in the Bible where the phrase is used to explain a decision not to expose someone: 'Then Joseph her husband, being a just man, and not willing to make her a publick example, was minded to put her away privily.'
provenance.significance: Matthew's logic is counter-intuitive and is the whole reason the phrase is memorable: Joseph is *therefore* unwilling to shame her — justice, in that sentence, is what restrains the just man from the public punishment he is entitled to exact. Mosiah 19:17 reproduces the structure exactly, and reproduces its oddity: 'Limhi was desirous that his father should not be destroyed; nevertheless, Limhi was not ignorant of the iniquities of his father, he himself, being a just man.' The clause explains a refusal to see a guilty man exposed and killed, by a son who knows precisely what his father has done. Recover Matthew 1:19 and the sentence is not saying that Limhi was righteous despite wanting to spare his father; it is saying that sparing him is what his righteousness consists in — which is a real claim, and one the chapter then overrules, since the people burn Noah anyway.

19:17.note: 'Limhi was desirous that his father should not be destroyed; nevertheless, Limhi was not ignorant of the iniquities of his father, he himself, being a just man.' A four-word KJV singleton used in the one office the KJV gives it. The 1830 'those that was with him' at 19:18 and 'those that was taken captive' at 19:16, both corrected in 1920, are the first edition's grammar throughout this stretch and are noted rather than argued.
19:17.text: Then Joseph her husband, being a just man, and not willing to make her a publick example, was minded to put her away privily.

provenance.other: No phrase is shared; the link is the shape of the curse and its fulfilment. Judges 9:20 is Jotham's curse — 'let fire come out from Abimelech, and devour the men of Shechem ... and let fire come out from the men of Shechem ... and devour Abimelech' — and Judges 9:49 reports the first half discharged, a thousand burned in the tower of Shechem, with 9:56 supplying the narrator's verdict: 'Thus God rendered the wickedness of Abimelech, which he did unto his father.'
provenance.significance: Jotham's curse is the only reciprocal fire-curse in the Bible: fire from the king to the people, and fire from the people back to the king. Mosiah 17:15-18 has Abinadi curse Noah's seed and priests with death by fire, and Mosiah 19:20 discharges it against Noah himself — 'they were angry with the king, and caused that he should suffer, even unto death by fire' — burned by the very men he had commanded to abandon their families. The first half of Abinadi's curse is not forgotten either; Alma 25:5-11 will report the priests' descendants burned. So the Book of Mormon has built its longest-running curse on the structure of the one in Judges 9, and has laid it over the same narrative that gave chapter 19 its tower and its Gideon. Whether the writer had Judges 9 open or had merely absorbed it, the two curses do the same work: they make the king's death a judicial act of the text rather than a political accident.

19:20.note: 'And they were angry with the king, and caused that he should suffer, even unto death by fire.' The death Abinadi promised at 17:18 in Ezekiel's and Jeremiah's words, delivered in the form of Judges 9. Catalogued as figural because there is no wording to test — kjvSpecific is therefore 'uncertain' rather than 'yes', since the borrowing, if it is one, is of a plot and not of an English sentence. It earns high confidence from the density of the rest of the Judges 9 material in this chapter (see 19:5), not from anything in this verse alone.
19:20.text: But if not, let fire come out from Abimelech, and devour the men of Shechem, and the house of Millo; and let fire come out from the men of Shechem, and from the house of Millo, and devour Abimelech.
